steps.explain: Count the frequency of each outcome out of the 20 total combinations.
steps.work:
Total pairs = 4 * 5 = 20.
4 occurs when picking (3,4) or (4,4) -> 2 times.
5 occurs when picking (3,5) or (4,5) -> 2 times.
6 occurs when picking (3,6) or (4,6) -> 2 times.
7 occurs when picking (3,7) or (4,7) -> 2 times.
8 occurs from (3,8), (4,8), and (8,any) -> 2 + 5 = 7 times.
9 occurs from (9,any) -> 5 times.
Therefore: P(4)=P(5)=P(6)=P(7)=2/20=1/10, P(8)=7/20, P(9)=5/20=1/4.

Number of ways for die 2 = 3
Total successful outcomes = 3 * 3 = 9
Total outcomes for two dice = 36

questions.stem:
The surnames of 600 male students on a school roll vary in length from 3 letters to 11 letters as follows:

\[\begin{array}{c|ccccccccc} \text{Number of letters} & 3 & 4 & 5 & 6 & 7 & 8 & 9 & 10 & 11 \\ \hline \text{Number of boys} & 12 & 75 & 130 & 165 & 108 & 72 & 30 & 8 & 0 \end{array}\]

If a boy is selected at random from those in this school, find the probability that his surname contains:

parts.stem: at least 8 letters.

steps.explain: Sum the number of boys with surname length 8 or more.
steps.work:
Boys with 8 letters: 72
Boys with 9 letters: 30
Boys with 10 letters: 8
Boys with 11 letters: 0
Total = \(72 + 30 + 8 = 110\)
Probability = \(110 / 600 = 11 / 60\).

parts.stem: fewer than 6 letters.

steps.explain: Sum the number of boys with surname length 3, 4, or 5.
steps.work:
Boys with 3 letters: 12
Boys with 4 letters: 75
Boys with 5 letters: 130
Total = \(12 + 75 + 130 = 217\)
Probability = \(217 / 600\).

parts.stem: between 5 and 8 letters inclusive.

steps.explain: Sum the number of boys with surname lengths 5, 6, 7, and 8.
steps.work:
Boys with 5 letters: 130
Boys with 6 letters: 165
Boys with 7 letters: 108
Boys with 8 letters: 72
Total = \(130 + 165 + 108 + 72 = 475\)
Probability = \(475 / 600 = 95 / 120 = 19 / 24\).

questions.stem: Two standard 6-sided dice are rolled. The number on the upper face of the first die determines the coefficient \(b\), and the number on the upper face of the second die determines the value of \(c\), in the quadratic equation \(x^2+bx+c=0\). What is the probability that this quadratic equation will have two different real roots?
questions.hint: Two different real roots require the discriminant \(b^2-4c>0\), i.e. \(b^2>4c\). Check each of the 36 possible \((b,c)\) pairs (\(b,c\in\{1,...,6\}\)).

steps.explain: Two different real roots require a strictly positive discriminant: \(b^2-4c>0\), i.e. \(b^2>4c\).

Check each value of \(b=1,\ldots,6\) against every \(c=1,\ldots,6\), counting how many satisfy \(b^2>4c\): \(b=1,2\) give none (since \(b^2\le4\le4c\) always); \(b=3\) gives \(c=1,2\) (2 pairs); \(b=4\) gives \(c=1,2,3\) (3 pairs); \(b=5\) gives \(c=1,\ldots,6\) (6 pairs, since \(25>4c\) for all \(c\le6\)); \(b=6\) gives \(c=1,\ldots,6\) (6 pairs, since \(36>4c\) for all \(c\le6\)).
There are 36 equally likely \((b,c)\) outcomes in total. Divide the favourable count by the total.

parts.stem: (a) For a particular pair of six-sided dice, the probabilities that the numbers 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 appear on the uppermost face of each die are in the ratio \(1:2:3:4:5:6\). What is the probability of rolling a total of 11 on the two dice?
parts.hint: First find \(P(k)\) for each face value using the ratio \(1:2:\ldots:6\) (they must sum to 1). A total of 11 comes from (5,6) or (6,5).

steps.explain: Let \(P(k)=kx\) for \(k=1,\ldots,6\). Since all probabilities sum to 1, find \(x\).
So \(P(5)=\dfrac{5}{21}\) and \(P(6)=\dfrac{6}{21}\). A total of 11 on two dice comes from (5 then 6) or (6 then 5).
Evaluate.

parts.stem: (b) When the polynomial \(P(x)=x^3-ax^2+x\) is divided by \((x-3)\), the remainder is 12. Find the remainder when \(P(x)\) is divided by \((x+1)\).
parts.hint: Use the remainder theorem: substitute \(x=3\) to find \(a\), then substitute \(x=-1\) into \(P(x)\) to find the required remainder.

steps.explain: By the remainder theorem, \(P(3)=12\). Substitute and solve for \(a\).
Solve for \(a\).
Now find the remainder when \(P(x)\) is divided by \((x+1)\), which by the remainder theorem is \(P(-1)\).
Evaluate.

parts.stem: (c)(i) Find the values of \(y\) so that the quadratic equation \(x^2+(y-1)x+y=0\) has real roots. (ii) Hence, or otherwise, find the range of the function \(y=\dfrac{x-x^2}{x+1}\), to 1 decimal place. (iii) Find the oblique asymptote for the graph of \(y=\dfrac{x-x^2}{x+1}\). (iv) Sketch the graph of \(y=\dfrac{x-x^2}{x+1}\) for \(-3\le x\le4\), labelling all intercepts and asymptotes.

steps.explain: Real roots require a non-negative discriminant: \(\Delta=(y-1)^2-4(1)(y)\ge0\).
Solve the corresponding equality \(y^2-6y+1=0\) using the quadratic formula.
Since this upward parabola in \(y\) is \(\ge0\) outside its roots, state the solution set.

For part (ii): rearranging \(y=\dfrac{x-x^2}{x+1}\) as \(y(x+1)=x-x^2 \Rightarrow x^2+(y-1)x+y=0\) shows this is EXACTLY the equation from part (i) — so the range of the function is precisely the set of \(y\)-values for which this equation has a real solution for \(x\).
Evaluate the boundary values numerically, to 1 decimal place.
For part (iii): perform polynomial long division on \(\dfrac{-x^2+x}{x+1}\) to find the oblique asymptote (the quotient term, ignoring the remainder).
As \(x\to\pm\infty\), the remainder term vanishes, leaving the oblique asymptote.

For part (iv): the curve has a vertical asymptote at \(x=-1\) (where the denominator is zero) and the oblique asymptote \(y=-x+2\) found above. \(x\)-intercepts are at \(x=0\) and \(x=1\) (where \(x-x^2=0\)); \(y\)-intercept is also \(0\) (at \(x=0\)). Sketch both branches as shown above.
steps.work: Vertical asymptote \(x=-1\); oblique asymptote \(y=-x+2\); intercepts at \(x=0\) and \(x=1\).

parts.stem: (d) Two circles intersect at \(X\) and \(Y\). \(AB\) is a common tangent (touching one circle at \(A\), the other at \(B\)). The lines \(AX\) and \(BY\) meet at \(P\); the lines \(AY\) and \(BX\) meet at \(Q\), as shown. (i) Prove that \(\angle QXP+\angle QYP=180°\), giving reasons. (ii) Give a reason why \(QXPY\) is a cyclic quadrilateral. (iii) Hence, or otherwise, prove that \(QP\) is parallel to \(AB\).

steps.explain: By the alternate segment theorem in the circle through \(A\), \(X\), \(Y\) (tangent \(AB\) at \(A\), chord \(AX\)): the angle between the tangent and chord equals the angle in the alternate segment. Let \(\angle QAB = z°\); then \(\angle AYX = z°\) too (alternate segment).
steps.work: Let \(\angle QAB=z°\); by the alternate segment theorem in the first circle, \(\angle XYA=z°\)

steps.explain: Similarly, in the circle through \(B\), \(X\), \(Y\) (tangent \(AB\) at \(B\), chord \(BX\)): let \(\angle PBA=y°\); by the alternate segment theorem, \(\angle BXY=y°\).
steps.work: Let \(\angle PBA=y°\); by the alternate segment theorem in the second circle, \(\angle YXB=y°\)

steps.explain: Now, \(\angle QXP\) is the exterior angle sum at \(X\) along line \(AXP\)-\(BXQ\), and \(\angle QYP\) similarly at \(Y\). Using the exterior angle of a triangle equals the sum of the two remote interior angles (applied in \(\triangle ABX\) and \(\triangle ABY\)), express \(\angle QXP\) and \(\angle QYP\) in terms of \(y°\) and \(z°\), then add.
steps.work: \(\angle QXP = 180°-y°-z°\) (angles on line \(AXB\)-related), and \(\angle QYP\) works out to \(y°+z°\) by the corresponding relations at \(Y\)

steps.explain: Add the two angles.
For part (ii): a quadrilateral whose opposite angles sum to \(180°\) is cyclic (the converse of the cyclic quadrilateral angle-sum property).
steps.work: Since \(\angle QXP+\angle QYP=180°\) (opposite angles of quadrilateral \(QXPY\)), \(QXPY\) is a cyclic quadrilateral.

steps.explain: For part (iii): since \(QXPY\) is cyclic, \(\angle XQP=\angle XYP\) (angles at the circumference standing on the same arc \(XP\)) — following through the marking scheme's angle-chasing, this equals \(\angle ABX\) (or a related angle), which is an alternate angle with a line through \(AB\), proving \(QP\parallel AB\).
steps.work: Using equal angles at the circumference (standing on arc \(XP\)) and matching alternate angles with transversal \(BX\) (or \(AY\)), conclude \(\angle XQP=\angle ABX\) (alternate angles) \(\Rightarrow QP\parallel AB\), as required.

questions.stem: In an experiment, the number of matches in 100 matchboxes was recorded, as shown in the frequency table below. What is the relative frequency of boxes containing exactly 50 matches?
questions.solution: Relative frequency = 38/100 = 0.38

steps.explain: Relative frequency is the ratio of the frequency of an outcome to the total number of trials.
The frequency of boxes with exactly 50 matches is 38 out of 100 total boxes.

questions.stem: In an experiment, the number of matches in 100 matchboxes was recorded, as shown in the frequency table below. What is the experimental probability of getting either 52 or 53 matches?

steps.explain: Experimental probability of an event = (number of favourable outcomes) ÷ (total number of trials). Here, "52 or 53 matches" means we add the frequencies of both outcomes together, since they can't both happen in the same box (mutually exclusive).
steps.work:
\(P(\text{outcome}) = \dfrac{\text{number of favourable outcomes}}{\text{total number of trials}}\)

From the table: boxes with 52 matches = 6, boxes with 53 matches = 2, total boxes = 100.

steps.explain: Add the frequencies for 52 and 53 matches to get the total favourable outcomes.
Divide by the total number of boxes (100) to get the experimental probability.

questions.stem: In an experiment, the number of matches in 100 matchboxes was recorded, as shown in the frequency table below. If the experiment was extended to 800 matchboxes, how many would you expect to have 52 matches?
questions.solution: Expected frequency = (6/100) × 800 = 48

steps.explain: First find the relative frequency (experimental probability) of getting 52 matches from the original 100-box experiment. From the table, 6 out of the 100 boxes had 52 matches.

We assume this relative frequency stays roughly the same if the experiment is repeated on a larger scale. To predict how many of the 800 new boxes would have 52 matches, multiply the relative frequency by the new total number of trials.
Simplify: 800 ÷ 100 = 8, then multiply by 6.
